subject: maths
title: KS2 Maths diagnostic
curriculum: National Curriculum in England, key stage 2 mathematics programme of study (2013), with the Year 6 SATs arithmetic and reasoning strands

skills.name: Number and place value
skills.why: Understanding place value, rounding and negative numbers makes every calculation easier and more accurate.
skills.strong: {name} understands place value well, including rounding and negative numbers.
skills.developing: {name} is secure with place value in smaller numbers but less sure with larger numbers and negatives.
skills.gap: {name} is not yet secure with place value. Almost every calculation depends on it, so it comes first.
skills.next_step: We will use number lines and place value charts to make large numbers feel manageable.

skills.name: Arithmetic
skills.why: Fast, accurate calculation supports every other topic, and it has its own paper in the Year 6 SATs.
skills.strong: {name} calculates quickly and accurately, including written methods for larger numbers.
skills.developing: {name} knows many number facts but makes slips with written methods, especially when exchanging.
skills.gap: {name} is not yet secure with times tables and written methods. These are used in every maths topic, so they are worth securing now.
skills.next_step: We will build times tables and written methods with short, regular practice.

skills.name: Fractions, decimals and percentages
skills.why: Fractions, decimals and percentages carry a lot of marks in Year 6 and are used throughout secondary maths.
skills.strong: {name} works confidently with fractions, decimals and percentages.
skills.developing: {name} understands simple fractions but is less sure comparing decimals or finding percentages.
skills.gap: {name} is not yet confident with fractions and decimals. These come up in almost every later topic, so they are worth building carefully.
skills.next_step: We will use visual models to make fractions and decimals click before practising calculations.

skills.name: Geometry and measures
skills.why: Shape, angles and measures are practical skills that give dependable marks in every test.
skills.strong: {name} works confidently with shapes, angles, perimeter and units of measure.
skills.developing: {name} knows shapes and units but is less sure with perimeter and angle facts.
skills.gap: {name} is not yet confident with measures and shape. These are used in everyday life as well as in tests, so they are worth practising.
skills.next_step: We will use drawings and real measuring to make these ideas concrete.

skills.name: Problem solving and reasoning
skills.why: Most test questions are word problems, so children need to choose the right maths, not just calculate.
skills.strong: {name} reads problems carefully and chooses the right steps, even in unfamiliar questions.
skills.developing: {name} solves one-step problems well but finds multi-step problems, missing numbers and ratio harder.
skills.gap: {name} is not yet confident turning a word problem into maths. This is where most test marks are, so it is worth real focus.
skills.next_step: We will practise breaking problems into steps and explaining our thinking out loud.

questions.ref: Y2/Y3: find 10 or 100 more or less than a given number
questions.stem: What is 10 more than 95?
questions.explain: 95 + 10 = 105. An answer of 96 means one was added instead of ten; 1,005 or 195 show confusion crossing the hundred.

questions.ref: Y3: add numbers with up to three digits
questions.stem: What is 46 + 38?
questions.explain: 46 + 38 = 84 (40 + 30 = 70, 6 + 8 = 14, 70 + 14 = 84). An answer of 74 means the ten from 6 + 8 was not carried.

questions.ref: Y2: recognise the equivalence of 2/4 and 1/2
questions.stem: Which fraction is the same as one half?
questions.explain: 2/4 is 2 out of 4 equal parts, which is the same as 1 out of 2. 1/4 is a common slip for 'half of a half'.

questions.ref: Y2: identify and describe the properties of 2-D shapes
questions.stem: How many sides does a hexagon have?
questions.explain: A hexagon has 6 sides. 5 (pentagon) and 8 (octagon) are the usual mix-ups.

questions.ref: Y3: solve problems involving money
questions.stem:
Apples cost 30p each.

How much do 3 apples cost, in pence?
questions.explain: 3 × 30p = 90p. An answer of 33 means the child added 30 and 3.

questions.ref: Y4: round any number to the nearest 10, 100 or 1,000
questions.stem: Round 367 to the nearest 10.
questions.explain: 367 is between 360 and 370, and 7 ones rounds up, so 370. 400 is rounding to the nearest hundred; 360 is rounding down.

questions.ref: Y3/Y4: recall multiplication facts up to 12 × 12
questions.stem: What is 7 × 8?
questions.explain: 7 × 8 = 56. 54 and 58 are typical recall slips; 15 means the child added.

questions.ref: Y3: find fractions of a set of objects
questions.stem: What is 1/4 of 24?
questions.explain: 24 ÷ 4 = 6. An answer of 12 means the child halved instead; 96 means they multiplied by 4.

questions.ref: Y3/Y4: convert between different units of measure
questions.stem: How many centimetres are there in 1 metre?
questions.explain: 1 m = 100 cm. 1,000 is millimetres in a metre (or metres in a kilometre), and 10 is millimetres in a centimetre.

questions.ref: Y3/Y4: solve comparison problems using information in tables
questions.stem:
Class 4 voted for their favourite fruit.

Apples: 8
Bananas: 12
Grapes: 5
Pears: 7

How many more children voted for bananas than for grapes?
questions.explain: 12 − 5 = 7. An answer of 17 means the child added; 12 means they read one value and stopped.

questions.ref: Y4: recognise the place value of each digit in a four-digit number
questions.stem: What is the value of the digit 7 in 3,726?
questions.explain: The 7 is in the hundreds column, so it is worth 700. Answering 7 means the child named the digit but not its value.

questions.ref: Y4: subtract with up to 4 digits using the formal written method
questions.explain: 1,000 − 358 = 642. Check: 358 + 642 = 1,000. An answer of 758 or 752 means the child subtracted the smaller digit from the larger in each column instead of exchanging.

questions.ref: Y5: read, write, order and compare numbers with up to 3 decimal places
questions.stem: Which of these numbers is the largest?
questions.explain: 0.54 has 5 tenths and 4 hundredths, the most. Choosing 0.405 or 0.45 means the child thinks more digits make a bigger number.

questions.ref: Y4: measure and calculate the perimeter of a rectilinear figure
questions.stem:
A rectangle is 8 cm long and 3 cm wide.

What is its perimeter, in cm?
questions.explain: 8 + 3 + 8 + 3 = 22 cm. 24 is the area (8 × 3), and 11 adds only two sides.

questions.ref: Y6: express missing number problems algebraically
questions.stem:
☐ × 4 + 5 = 33

What number goes in the box?
questions.explain: Work backwards: 33 − 5 = 28, then 28 ÷ 4 = 7. Check: 7 × 4 + 5 = 33. An answer of 9.5 comes from dividing 38 by 4 (adding 5 instead of subtracting).

questions.ref: Y6: use negative numbers in context, and calculate intervals across 0
questions.stem:
The temperature is −3°C. It rises by 8 degrees.

What is the temperature now, in °C?
questions.explain: Counting up 8 from −3 gives 5 (3 steps to 0, then 5 more). An answer of 11 or −11 means the child ignored the negative sign.

questions.ref: Y6: multiply a 2-digit number by a 2-digit number using long multiplication
questions.stem: What is 36 × 24?
questions.explain: 36 × 24 = 36 × 20 + 36 × 4 = 720 + 144 = 864. An answer of 216 means the tens row (36 × 20) was calculated as 36 × 2.

questions.ref: Y6: solve problems involving the calculation of percentages
questions.stem: What is 15% of 80?
questions.explain: 10% of 80 = 8 and 5% = 4, so 15% = 12. An answer of 68 means the child found 80 − 12 (a 15% decrease).

questions.ref: Y5: know angles on a straight line add up to 180°
questions.stem:
Two angles sit next to each other on a straight line. One of them is 65°.

What is the size of the other angle, in degrees?
questions.explain: Angles on a straight line add up to 180°, so 180 − 65 = 115°. An answer of 25 uses 90° (a right angle) instead of 180°; 295 uses 360°.

questions.ref: Y6: solve problems involving unequal sharing and grouping using ratio
questions.stem:
In a class, the ratio of boys to girls is 2 : 3. There are 30 children in the class.

How many girls are there?
questions.explain: 2 + 3 = 5 parts, so each part is 30 ÷ 5 = 6. Girls are 3 parts: 3 × 6 = 18. An answer of 12 is the number of boys, and 20 comes from treating the ratio as the fraction 2/3.
